topic:overview:why:body: Agriculture covers 40% of U.S. land and accounts for approximately 80% of consumptive water use. However these impacts are large due to the scale of production. U.S. farmers produce more than any other country besides India and China and twice as much as they did in 1970. Without efficiency improvements, this level of production would have far larger impacts.
topic:overview:happened:body: Following a trajectory of sustainable intensification, the environmental intensity of agriculture—the resource use or environmental impacts per unit of production—has fallen nearly across the board. Since 1990, farm output rose more than 50% while greenhouse gas emissions rose only 8 percent and land use and water withdrawals both fell. In some cases total impacts have declined; in others rising impacts have been far outpaced by increasing production.
topic:overview:chart:0:title: Agricultural output, resource use, and impacts
topic:nitrogen:happened:body: Nitrogen surplus—the nitrogen added to cropland but not removed in crops—rose sharply through the 1970s before plateauing. Nitrogen-use efficiency, the share of nitrogen taken up by crops, started to reach over 70% in 2016. This has helped shrink the Gulf dead zone, though it is still larger than EPA's goal.

topic:nitrogen:why:body: Nitrogen not taken up by crops can contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, drinking-water contamination, and algal blooms. In the Gulf, nutrient-fueled blooms can drain oxygen from bottom waters, creating a summer dead zone where aquatic life struggles to survive.
topic:water:title: With better irrigation, water use plateaued
topic:water:happened:body: Irrigation and livestock withdrawals rose until 1980 before plateauing and falling. As agricultural output grew, withdrawals per unit of farm output fell by more than half. Yet regional challenges persist, with water levels in some aquifers still falling.
study:water:description: Volume of water use per unit of product
topic:soil:why:body: Erosion removes fertile topsoil, carries sediment and nutrients into waterways, and can undermine long-term productivity. Keeping soil in place supports both yields and water quality.
topic:practices:chart:1:subtitle: Less disturbance and more winter cover help curb erosion and retain moisture, though cover crops typically reduce yields.

topic:rd:happened:body: From its 2002 peak to 2024, public agricultural R&D fell 26 percent after inflation. R&D intensity—spending as a percent of the sector's value—has fallen even more: about 45% since 2002. Agricultural productivity growth has subsequently slowed, though it is influenced by other factors too.
topic:climate:happened:body: Direct U.S. agricultural emissions were 595 million metric tons CO2e in 2023, 8 percent above 1990. Estimates by economic sector, which includes on-farm fuel use, are higher. Yet declining emissions per pound and bushel have limited growth in total emissions.
topic:nitrogen:title: Efficiency improvements help shrink the Gulf dead zone
topic:herbicides:happened:body: From the early 1990s to 2015, acute toxicity quotients declined for four of the five crops studied, while chronic hazard quotients declined for two. Much of the acute improvement came as hazardous products like alachlor and cyanazine were phased out.
topic:soil:happened:body: Conservation tillage, cover cropping, contour farming, and related practices helped lower both water and wind erosion. Most of the decline occurred in the 1980s and 1990s. Erosion rates have since leveled off.

topic:rd:why:body: Public agricultural research is the largest driver of productivity growth, improving yields, resource efficiency, and environmental performance. Since its benefits can take decades to emerge, sustained investment is critical.

topic:livestock:why:body: Selective breeding, better nutrition and feeding, disease control, improved housing, and mechanization help producers obtain more output from feed and animals. Larger and more specialized operations make some of these practices easier to use. These shifts cut the environmental footprint of each major livestock product.
topic:livestock:happened:body: Broilers need much less feed per pound while reaching heavier weights at younger ages. Pig litters have grown. And dairies have widely adopted productivity-enhancing technologies, particularly automated milking and feeding, through use of the yield-enhancing rBST hormone declined.

topic:practices:why:body: Adopting improved seeds, precision equipment, and other agricultural technologies and practices helps farmers produce more food while using fewer resources and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, and other environmental impacts.
topic:practices:happened:body: Farmers rapidly adopted genetically engineered seeds, now planted on over 90% of U.S. corn, soybean, and cotton acreage. No- and reduced-till farming and more efficient irrigation systems have also expanded substantially, while several precision agriculture technologies remain less widely adopted.
